utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Registrar, could you call the case, please. One moment, because I notice that the accused is not here as yet. One moment. Let's wait. He is not going to be here. Okay. Okay. All right. I thought for a moment that he had come over for this interesting hearing. Let's proceed. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84-PT, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj Idriz Balaj and Lahi Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Registrar. Let's go straight to appearances. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: My name is Moore, I'm a Senior Trial Attorney. I'm assisted by my learned friend Mr. Gilles Dutertre and Ms. Sandra D'Angelo. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and good afternoon to you and your team. Appearances for the accused Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: My name is Ben Emmerson, and I appear with Mr. Rodney Dixon and Mr. Michael O'Reilly on behalf of Mr. Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Emmerson, and good afternoon to you and your team. The purpose of this particular hearing is to complete the submissions on the Defence motion filed on the 15th of August on behalf of accused Ramush Haradinaj requesting reassessment of conditions of provisional release and the ensuing Prosecution response to the said motion, which response was filed on the 12th of September, and the report from the Special Representative of the Secretary-General, Mr. Soren Jessen-Petersen for UNMIK to the Registrar of this Tribunal, and lastly the confidential Defence reply to UNMIK's submission and to the Prosecution response to the Defence motion which was filed, I understand, a few hours ago and a copy of which we have received before -- prior to this hearing. It doesn't mean to see that we haven't read it. We have gone through it already, so we are throughly au courant with its contents. The idea of having an oral hearing to deal with the Defence motion and the successive documents, judicial acts that have been filed, is not because the documents that have been filed itself are not exhaustive or are not clear in themselves. In fact, they are extremely clear, exhaustive in what they seek to bring to the knowledge of the Trial Chamber. It's also because now that there has been a complete exchange of opinions between the two parties and also, and I must thank the representative of UNMIK here, a response from UNMIK in time to put the Trial Chamber in a position to deal with this matter without delay, we think that the best way of dealing with this manner -- with this matter is to give it the greatest transparency possible without, of course, the need to repeat unduly some of the points, but primarily so to give the opportunity to the two parties to put questions to the representative of UNMIK, if it's the case, particularly since in view of some of the parts contained in the Prosecution's response there seems to be some -- an indication of some questions that might be solicited. And in any case, also to give you an opportunity to exchange further your views, particularly now that we have also a final response from the Defence to the response of the Prosecution. The idea was to give first the floor to one of the Defence counsel. I would imagine it's you, Mr. Emmerson, to give a very brief expose of your position, your request, as contained in your motion but taking into consideration what happened afterwards. You will be followed by and intervention from, I would imagine, Mr. Moore, and then finally we would also give the floor to the representative for UNMIK, and then of course if there are any leftovers, as I would suspect there would be, we will go through those in due course. I had in mind giving you something like ten, maximum 15 minutes each, but please try to stick to that time frame. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, may I begin by expressing my personal thanks for the consideration that the Chamber has shown in maintaining the date for this afternoon's hearing, which I know caused some difficulties. Your Honours, as you know, the Defence are applying for a variation of the conditions of provisional release as envisaged in the Chamber's decision of the 6th of June so as to lift the restriction on Mr. Haradinaj's involvement in public political activity and to enable him to play a greater role in public life in Kosovo. When the Chamber imposed the current condition, it did so on the express basis that the necessity for the restriction would be reassessed after 90 days on the basis of the experience gained during that time. Now, the Defence understood --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel slow down, please, for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: More slowly. Your Honours, the Defence understood the purpose of that condition, I hope correctly, as reflecting the Chamber's intention that Mr. Haradinaj should be removed from the political equation in Kosovo for a period long enough to establish a calm transition for his provisional release, and as you know, the Defence interpreted the condition strictly and produced a written protocol which was designed to ensure that both the spirit and the letter of the Chamber's condition were clearly met. Your Honours, the experience to date has, we say, entirely vindicated the trust which the Chamber placed in Mr. Haradinaj. Consistent with his responsible approach throughout these proceedings, he has complied in full with the restriction on his political activities, confining himself to administration and organisational activities within his party, and he has cooperated with the implementation of a detailed reporting regime which has enabled UNMIK closely to monitor all the conditions of his provisional release including this one. Given that the current timetable for this case makes it apparent that Mr. Haradinaj will remain on provisional release for at least another year and possibly longer, in our submission the time is now right for a modest relaxation in the current conditions to enable him to participate more fully in political life in Kosovo. It is important, briefly, to spell out what that means. Mr. Haradinaj is not asking that he should be allowed to hold any governmental position or to represent Kosovo in the upcoming status talks, but he is asking that he should be free to express his political views in public. That means two things. First, it means a continuation of his consistent message that the future of Kosovo can only be secured within the framework of international law and in full cooperation with international institutions; and secondly, it means a continuation of his unqualified support for the full integration of national minorities. And in those two vital respects, he is in a position to make an important and we say valuable contribution to Kosovo at a time in Kosovo's history when his views are likely to carry weight. We recognise that. Contrary to the submissions in the Prosecution motion, Mr. Haradinaj has never made any secret of his wish to contribute in that way. Indeed, he made just such a contribution in the dignified speech that he delivered at the funeral of his brother Enver in April of this year when he was first and briefly provisionally released, calling for cooperation and calm at a particularly volatile moment. And it is a consistent theme of those informed observers who have watched Kosovo closely since March of this year that Mr. Haradinaj's stance in response to the indictment and his conduct throughout has been a source of stability in the region rather than the reverse. May I go briefly into closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go to closed or private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The Prosecution in its motion appears to call the independence of the Special Representative into question in some way. Given Mr. Petersen's seniority as a diplomat reporting directly to the Secretary-General that is a surprising position for the Prosecution to take. As the Prosecution itself points out Mr. Petersen holds Mr. Haradinaj in high regard precisely because of his achievements in office while he was Prime Minister. And, again, the Defence would emphasise that this direct experience and close knowledge of the conditions in Kosovo places UNMIK in best possible position to assist the Chamber on this question. But no doubt Mr. Rossin can elaborate on those questions. The Prosecution for its part relies in its motion on a statement to the opposite effect made by Mr. Dusan Janic, the coordinator of the Forum for Ethnic Relations in Belgrade. No doubt this gentleman's views are entitled to respect, but as a prominent representative of Belgrade, he can hardly be characterised as an independent judge in these matters and his opinion cannot, in our submission, begin to carry the weight which attaches to the considered assessment of the Secretary-General's Special Representative. Mr. President, against that background I would like, if I may, to address four specific arguments raised by the Prosecution. First, the Prosecution submits that if Mr. Haradinaj were permitted to play any role in public life, this would somehow empty the other conditions of provisional release of their content. They suggest, for example, that it would be impossible for UNMIK to monitor Mr. Haradinaj's movements because a politician's diary is unpredictable. They suggest that UNMIK would be unable to fulfil its obligation and commitment to arrest Mr. Haradinaj in the event of a breach because his political capital would be too high. Mr. President, again the surprising and unsupported assertions run directly counter to the evidence submitted by UNMIK. May I go into private session again very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course Mr. Haradinaj's involvement in public life will require sensitive handling, but as UNMIK can confirm, he has conducted himself thus far with the utmost discretion in the political arena. When the Chamber in its June decision contemplated a possible relaxation of this condition, it stipulated that any application would be decided in the light of experience, and that experience has been, we say, uniformly positive. The only concrete instance which the Prosecution can point to as evidence of non-cooperation was when Mr. Haradinaj was seen outside his home on the 7th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't labour of those. They are more or less minor incidents and they were not followed by any connotation on the part of the Prosecution, such as asking for the revocation.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I wouldn't labour those. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I shan't in those circumstances. Your Honour, the second argument the Prosecution puts forward is if this application were granted it would have an intimidating effect on victims and witnesses. That is, the application to permit his involvement in public political life. But as the Chamber will recall, the Prosecution has previously submitted that the mere fact of his provisional release would have an indirect effect of making witnesses feel less safe and that submission was rejected by the Chamber, and in our submission experience to date shows the Chamber was right. The Prosecution has been quite unable to point to any instance in which a witness has been intimidated or even reluctant in coming forward as a result of the provisional release decision. Indeed, it is difficult imagine, we say, an accused who could have done more to reassure potential witnesses of their safety. As we point out in our written response to the Prosecution's motion filed this morning, Mr. Haradinaj has taken steps at every possible stage to ensure that witnesses feel safe to come forward. He has complete confidence in the Tribunal's ability to establish the truth, and he has made public statements reassuring potential witnesses through his lawyers that they should feel free to come forward and give evidence, and with that end in mind, as we point out, he has now appointed an internationally supervised investigation team of the highest possible calibre to ensure that the Defence case can be prepared without any risk of witnesses feeling unsafe or intimidated. In short, we say the Prosecution have failed to put forward any concrete reason to believe that restricting Mr. Haradinaj's involvement in public life is necessary to ensure witness safety. Indeed, if UNMIK believed that the two were in any way incompatible, the Special Representative would hardly have made the submissions that he has done. Your Honours, moving swiftly, the third argument raised by the Prosecution relates to the suggested relaxation in the geographical limits on Mr. Haradinaj's freedom of movement. Again, the Prosecution seems to be suggesting that he has made a secret of his motives. That is not the case. Plainly this application is linked to the application to lift restrictions on his political activities. If he is to play a part in public life, then we say it is appropriate that he be able to travel in Kosovo, at least to the extent of visiting the main sites of support for his own political party. Again, it's UNMIK's clear position that a relaxation of that condition would not undermine its ability to supervise and implement terms of provisional release. Other matters relating to the geographical condition are addressed in our written submission of this morning. Finally, Mr. President, I should say a word with the Prosecution's application for an adjournment on the ground that further investigations are being conducted. Given the current state of the evidence in this case, it comes as no surprise to the Defence to learn that the Prosecution is still seeking further material. That process will no doubt continue for some time to come, but it is no reason, we say, to adjourn the current application which has been foreshadowed and of which the Prosecution have had notice in effect since the provisional release decision on the 6th of June, and for all those reasons we respectfully invite you to allow the application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Emmerson, and thank you also for staying within the 15 minutes. In fact, you took 13 minutes. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Might I at the very outset deal with the second matter that my learned friend Mr. Emmerson has dealt with. Firstly, may I remind the Court that the Court, when passing its judgement in relation to the earlier application, said specifically that the accused could pose -- or that there had been no evidence shown that the accused could pose a concrete danger to anyone, including victims and witnesses. Clearly in our reply, in paragraph 13, there is reference made in elipitcal form, and I accept that, that the Prosecution, in our submission, is now in a position to place before the Court in ex parte proceedings material that we would submit would negate that particular concern made by the -- or expressed by the Court. Obviously given the circumstances of that material, it is not something that we submit should go into the public domain, but this matter has been looked at with considerable care, and we would therefore make application for this matter to be placed before the Court for the Court's evaluation when considering not only this particular motion but perhaps with regard to provisional release as a whole. And therefore, I would make application at this time for the Court to hear such matters by way of ex parte application. And I'm entirely in the Court's hands about how that could be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but in the meantime let's proceed on the rest, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I can't proceed on the rest because, quite simply, what we are submitting are that there are four specific instances where the Prosecution have material before them which indicate that on two occasions witnesses have been influenced and approached by parties, and I'm not going to go into the detail, in relation to them giving evidence in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now can you reasonably expect the Trial Chamber or the Pre-Trial Chamber to seriously take this into consideration if the details and the information is not disclosed to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We would submit that firstly there are proceedings which can be undertaken, because the Court are the custodians of the liberty of any defendant. But nevertheless, while the defendant has rights, so have witnesses. And I cannot possibly place within the public domain the material that I have which by our judgement would place those particular people's liberty and perhaps lives at risk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you're not even conceding at least as has been done in other cases that given that the material will not be disclosed to the accused himself at least it is disclosed to the -- to his attorneys, to his -- to Defence counsel. Surely if you have reasons to doubt whether it would be wisdom -- the wisdom of disclosing this material to the accused himself, you shouldn't have any doubt as to whether it should be disclosed to his Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It is not a case of mistrusting or having concerns for the integrity of Defence counsel. It is the fact that we in the Office of the Prosecutor have an obligation to the security of witnesses, for their safety. We have information to suggest that their safety has been placed at risk already, and by disclosing additional information, in our judgement it would be an unacceptable risk to these individuals who have come before the Court in the sense that they are willing to give evidence to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me stop you here for the time being, Mr. Moore, and give back the floor to Mr. Emmerson should he wish to respond to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, we respectfully say that the Chamber should proceed on the basis of the open material adduced before it. I'm not sure, with the greatest of respect to Mr. Moore, that he truly appreciates what an extensive departure he is proposing from the principles of fair trial, inter partes, adversarial justice. In a brief conversation when he notified me this application before coming into court, he suggested it might be modelled on an ex parte procedure used in English criminal courts for determining whether evidence should be disclosed to the Defence in a jury trial in circumstances, where if the evidence is not disclosed it plays no part in the proceedings analogous to the Rule in Rule 66(C) of this Tribunal's Rules, that there can be an ex parte hearing in order to determine disclosure. But what Mr. Moore is inviting Chamber to do is to act as a Tribunal of fact relying on closed material without there being any fair opportunity for the opposing party to see it, understand it, and respond to it and indeed that the only authority that I am aware one, and it is one I would have brought to you if I'd had proper notice of this application, is decision of the European Court of Human Rights in Edwards and Lewis against the United Kingdom some three or four years ago now holding that precisely such a situation is a breach of Article 6. And so with the greatest of respect, if Mr. Moore does not wish to rely on the material in open session, then he must abandon reliance upon it, and as I understand it, that is his position. Unless he is able to persuade Your Honours to see him in private and to have only one party to the proceedings present and represented and persuading you to act on a particular substantive material, then the Office of the Prosecutor will not rely on the material, and we say that is a choice for them to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is a matter of personal liberty of an individual given that he already has provisional release, but it's still question of personal liberty. With all due respect, I wouldn't speak of -- of fair trial at this stage. I don't think we have reached that as yet. But your request, Mr. Moore, is tantamount to inviting the Chamber to peruse the records of these investigations in secret, never allowing even a shred of information to be leaked to the Defence and then come down with a decision for or against the Defence motion based on information to which they have never been made privy, and I will just have a simple answer, you know, a response from the Trial Chamber saying that your request is upheld -- or your request is postponed pending the outcome of some investigations that are being conducted by the Prosecution, but sorry, we can't tell you what they are and that's the extent. I mean, it's -- we're talking of someone else's liberty here, personal freedom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We -- we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anything -- at least we could have discussion behind closed doors, but -- about the contents of -- or the substance of these investigations, but not to the extent that it should -- any discussion should be held between you, the Office of the Prosecutor, and us, the three Judges, and it's as if, you know, I mean, it's not in their interest to know what's going on. I think it's very much in the interest of each and every Defence counsel in every case to know if there is a grounded suspicion that his or their client or persons associated to their client is or are or may be involved in activities like the ones you seem to indicate. I mean, it's -- I would be the first one as a Defence counsel to expect to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I as a practitioner both prosecuting and defence, admit that witnesses have rights also. It's important to remember the fundamental that this is not a Trial Chamber that is exclusively dealing with the rights of a defendant. Witnesses have rights as well. They have a right to protection. They have a right to life in the extreme case. Therefore, I would be failing in my duty if I revealed material which by its very nature would disclose the identity of those witnesses either by way of name or by way of description which would lead to their identification. And consequently, we submit firstly that there is material that we have that suggests that Mr. Haradinaj has been involved, since provisional release, in witness intimidation. I equally, without going into detail, would submit that we are at what I will call a preliminary stage, and unfortunately investigations take time. It is the Prosecution intention to try and clarify these matters, to see whether in actual fact there is merit or validity within the information that we have, but we cannot disclose the information that would reveal their identitu at this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And it is a question of balance, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We have heard what you have to say, Mr. Moore. Please proceed to submit -- make your submissions on the rest of the Defence motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In any event --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have course come back to you on this -- on this issue. We are not deciding it. But it's definitely not going to hold at least the discussions for today, and then we will discuss it amongst ourselves and see how much weight to give it at this present moment and point out to you should there be the need for the -- for handing over these documents to the Tribunal under which conditions that will be done. But I think we can safely say that we do not envisage at the present moment a situation where we decide an issue on matters that are not put before the Defence. I'm not saying the accused. At least Defence counsel to at least put them in a position where they can defend their client.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I, of course, am fully bound by what the Court's observations are. In any event, may I formally make an application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I've made a note already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I make an application that in actual fact this matter could be deferred for one month to facilitate further investigations in relation to these matters. It may well be in the intervening time that the Court may well, shall we say, for example, indicate, well, such matters should be disclosed to the Defence. It may be that there will be additional matters found. But I will in any event make a formal application for a one month's adjournment in relation to the material that we have in our possession. We would submit that given the -- it's important to remember that the allegations here are grave and weighty, as indeed all matters that come before this Court. What is submitted here, of course, is that this defendant has been involved in crimes where he has exercised control over other parties without direct participation himself. I am fully aware of the judge -- of the Court's ruling in relation to the fact that there is no concrete material that the Court can rely upon in relation to concerns of witnesses. All we would submit is quite simply this: Firstly, that by permitting Mr. Haradinaj to resume what I will call political activity where visual and newspaper disclosure will clearly raise his profile, and I mean no criticism by that, will of itself and inferentially affect the ongoing investigations because of the fear of -- whether justifiable or not, of witnesses when they are coming to give statements against Mr. Haradinaj and others. And secondly, and again perhaps this relates to the material now that the Prosecution have, weaken the resolve of witnesses who are already prepared to give evidence but because of the fears that they have and the exposure that Mr. Haradinaj would have in relation to his political involvement that they themselves may well indicate and perhaps have indicated that they would not wish to give evidence for this Tribunal. And therefore the loadstar of any deliberation for this Appeals Chamber -- or this Court may be surely a fair trial, and a fair trial must also involve a fair trial to the witnesses and ensuring their protection, that they can give evidence without oppression, to give evidence in a fair and reasoned way. For Mr. Haradinaj to resume his political activity, we submit is one step beyond the Rubicon and as such should not be permitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Moore. Sir, you will forgive me, you will pardon me for having overlooked at the early opening stages of this hearing to ask you to announce your presence here as representative of UNMIK. Could you please do that now, and my apologies to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROSSIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour, and thank you, members of the Court, for inviting me to represent UNMIK today, the UN interim administration in Kosovo. My name is Larry Rossin, Lawrence Rossin. I'm the Principal Deputy Special Representative of the Secretary-General for Kosovo and the deputy head of UNMIK, the interim administration mission in Kosovo. I appeared also at the hearing here in late May on Mr. Haradinaj's provisional release request. If I might, I should first recall very briefly what I said then about the authority of UNMIK in this matter in Kosovo. UNMIK is the United Nations body with responsibility for the interim administration of Kosovo under UN Security Council Resolution 1244, 1999. As such UNMIK has the authority --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the UNMIK representative please be asked to slow down for the benefit of the interpreters and/or distribute the text that he's reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The interpreters have rightly asked me to intervene and ask you to slow down a little bit or else if you have a copy of the text from which you are reading to make it available to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROSSIN
utterances.text: I'll be very brief and I'll -- [B/C/S on English channel].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think there is the Serbian interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Rossin, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROSSIN
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. UNMIK will therefore fulfil to its maximum capacity any requirements that may be established by the Tribunal. With regard to the September 1st letter from the Special Representative of the Secretary-General to the Registrar of the Tribunal, we presented at the request of this court UNMIK's assessment of the two requests made by the -- in the Defence motion of 5 August 2005 on behalf of Mr. Haradinaj, and I would just make a few key points out of that. First of all, since his provisional release into UNMIK's custody on 9 June, it's UNMIK's assessment that Mr. Haradinaj has been in full compliance with the terms of the decision granted by the Trial Chamber on 6 June. We've reported this to the Registrar bi-weekly as required by the Court. Secondly, UNMIK confirms that it would have the capacity to supervise the involvement of Mr. Haradinaj in political activities under the terms specified in paragraph 9 of the Defence motion were the Tribunal to so amended his order for provisional release. Thirdly, UNMIK has stated its generally positive expectation of the impact of Mr. Haradinaj's political activity were the Court to vary that condition. Fourthly, with regard to the terms which concern the movement of Mr. Haradinaj within Kosovo, UNMIK has no objection to and is in a position to implement what is requested in the Defence motion should the Court so amended his order for provisional release except with regard to paragraph 27(B) which we stated in the letter. And with regard -- with regard to that subparagraph, in order for UNMIK to provide an adequate level of personal protection for Mr. Haradinaj, a reasonable amount of advance notice must be provided for security purposes for any movement within the two locations concerned. A period of 24 hours advance notice to UNMIK should in our view be maintained. However, as we've described to the Court, a minimum of one hour advance notice could be acceptable in exceptional circumstances. I would thank you for your time and consideration, Your Honour, and am prepared to respond to any questions you have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you, Mr. Rossin. Are there any particular questions that either of you would like to make, to put to Mr. Rossin?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is one matter that I would like to address you to, Mr. Rossin. The document or the report or response of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General for Kosovo of the 1st September addresses the Defence motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROSSIN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It does not, of course, or it couldn't address the concerns that have been indicated, raised in the Prosecution response.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROSSIN
utterances.text: That's correct. Your request came before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. And there are some concerns. They are more or less related personally to the figure of Mr. Jessen-Petersen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROSSIN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is also what I would describe as a sort of subtle hint that sort of UNMIK is too forthcoming in this area. And thirdly, this other matter that has been raised today which, if true, of course, is of the utmost importance and gravity, that is the allegation that has been made in court today by Mr. Moore, which I need not repeat, details which of course we don't have, I don't have, my colleagues don't have, and neither you, I suppose, nor the Defence team. Do you wish to contribute anything on UNMIK's part? Remember, please, that you are here representing UNMIK and not in a personal capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROSSIN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct. I don't speak personally in this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not trying to teach you, I mean, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROSSIN
utterances.text: Thank you. With regard, first of all, to your first question about Mr. Jessen-Petersen's personal role or his personal expressions that were quoted also in the Prosecution document, Mr. Jessen-Petersen and indeed all of us in UNMIK had long relations with Mr. Haradinaj in his various political and governmental roles over the past years. Our experience with him at all stages, and particularly in his brief period as Prime Minister of Kosovo, were quite positive. The SRSG, Mr. Jessen-Petersen, has a number of responsibilities under the 1244 mandate to create stability, to move Kosovo forward, to build institutions of responsible self-government, to empower those institutions, to move Kosovo forward towards facilitating the political process for final status, and within that things like building security, building multi-ethnicity and so forth. In all of those areas, our experience with Mr. Haradinaj was very constructive. He took a leadership role in many of those areas during his period in government, and that's what Mr. Jessen-Petersen has repeatedly referred to in his public statements. It's obviously not meant in any way to comment on the merits or the substance of the charges that have been brought or the trial itself. That's a matter for the Court to decide. We don't have an opinion in that regard. It's not for us to have an opinion. Secondly, with regard to UNMIK being too forthcoming, we do have in the Resolution an obligation to cooperate with the Tribunal and the Special Representative and all of us have interpreted that broadly; that is to say, whatever facilitates the work of the court and all of those things are matters of the Court and in our understanding is something we should do. So if we have the ability to provide guarantees or to respond to requirements of the court, whether it's monitoring the movements, providing for the security, whatever it may be of somebody who is released, telling the Court what we can do in that regard before it makes a decision so it can have an informed decision, we view it as our obligation to come proactively or certainly in response to your inquiries, the Court's inquiries, to provide that information. With regard, for example, to talking about Mr. Haradinaj's in this case, this particular defendant's political role and our assessment of the role he would be likely to play were he to be released, I think two comments. One is when we talk about constructive, constructive is to find --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Rossin please slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROSSIN
utterances.text: Sorry. Is to find against the standards of the Special Representative's responsibilities under 1244. Constructive it further those responsibilities, and that is our assessment. Secondly, we would make that assessment that that is the case. We are not advocating that Mr. Haradinaj should play a role. That's not really for us to do. What we're describing is our belief of the consequences and the nature of the role he would play were he allowed to do so by your decision. And, thirdly, with regard to the third matter, we have no information. I talked with our police obviously as I was preparing to come up here. We've sent bi-weekly reports from the police as well as from myself with regard to paragraph 9, or the paragraph in the decision that talks about his political activity, and if there were any information that we had had from any source concerning any activity related to witnesses, that obviously would have been very serious and something we would have reported. Our police, I know, have talked -- I talked with the Registrar's office this morning and a general discussion have relationships with responsibilities towards witnesses that -- that frankly I know little about other than we have those responsibilities to provide protection, and our police have mentioned nothing to me of any such information reaching them. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. It doesn't mean to say that if he is not privy to any such information that annihilates, neutralises what you allege in your response, Mr. Moore. I'm making that clear. In other words -- yes. I think we can stop here unless there are further submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether you would allow me just to say a few words in final response to the procedural issues that have been raised as far as the closed material is concerned. I appreciate that the Chamber is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Go ahead, Mr. Emmerson, provided you keep it as short as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'll keep it as short as I possibly can. Whether this is a fair trial situation or not, what Mr. Moore was suggesting in his submissions was that the considerations to which he has drawn attention could in a final analysis result in an application to revoke Mr. Haradinaj's provisional release. So on any view the procedure that is adopted in the context of what Mr. Moore is suggesting is a procedure which would have to withstand the requirements necessary for withdrawing an individual's liberty from them, and so to that extent, the fair procedure requirements are not as we respectfully submit materially different. Secondly, this is a series of complaints which come -- or concerns which come very late in the day with no particulars at all after all the parties have prepared on a particular basis. Your Honour suggested as one possible solution the potential for disclosure to Defence counsel, and I should simply like, if I may, to respond to that by reference, and I appreciate this is only one source of guidance in an unchartered area, but by reference to national procedure. The position in United Kingdom law at least is it is considered a breach of professional ethics now for a counsel to receive material on a counsel-to-counsel basis, partly because it undermines the confidentiality of the lawyer/client relationship and the confidence that the one can have in the other, and partly because in order to be able to make any informed submissions to the Court on the substance of the material, I would need to be in the position to take my client's instructions on them. So what we do respectfully submit is that as we stand here today, it is quite clear that the Prosecution are not suggesting to you that they are in a position to allege or provide evidence of any of these matters. If they are at some subsequent stage, and it inspires little confidence that they don't know it's three months as in their motion on Monday or a month as in the oral submissions this afternoon, but if they really are to be in a position at some stage concretely to advance matters adversarial and inter partes, then that is the time to do it and to do it properly in a further motion in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Would the position change from the professional ethics point of view if your client gave his consent for this counsel to counsel --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Domestically it would not, but plainly domestic procedure is not the guiding consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because it has been done here. It has been the practice here, and we've -- I have myself adopted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. There is a quite --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're not the only one. It has been adopted here from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There is quite separate procedure in UK domestic law which has been introduced to address this problem which is for the court itself to appoint a security vetted counsel to represent the interests of the accused without acting for the individual concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we ought to give more time to this issue. Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I just indicate, and I'm grateful for my learned friend Mr. Emmerson indicating what the national considerations are in our jurisdiction. For my part it is a new law and clearly it's beneficial if a route can be obtained which will ensure a fair hearing for all parties. If in actual fact there is the possibility of an independent counsel to protect the interests of the defendant, I'm quite sure that the Prosecution would look very sympathetically towards that, but clearly I have to take instructions in relation to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And this is virgin ground as far as I'm concerned, so I would rather reserve my position and that of my colleagues and we'll come back to you on this matter later on. The hearing is adjourned. And we will hand down our decision as soon as we have reached an agreement. Thank you.
